summaries.example: Imagine saying, “If the card is a club, then it is a king.” If the card is not a club, should the statement count as true, false, or neither? One idea says the bet is simply called off, so the statement is neither true nor false. This helps explain why some logicians use three values instead of only true and false.
summaries.summary:
Conditionals are sentences such as “If A, then B.” The entry asks what makes such sentences true, false, reasonable to say, or undecided. A very simple approach uses only two values, true and false. It treats a conditional as false when its first part is true but its second part is false. This is useful for mathematics and formal proofs, but it can make odd claims seem acceptable. For example, if the first part is false, almost any second part can make the conditional count as true. It also does not capture the special way people talk about imagined situations.

One important alternative uses three values: true, false, and a third value often described as void or indeterminate. On a version associated with de Finetti, “If A, then B” is true when both A and B are true, false when A is true and B is false, and indeterminate when A is false. This resembles a bet that is canceled when the condition for the bet does not occur. Other three-valued systems treat the middle value differently and therefore support different rules of inference. For instance, some preserve Modus Ponens—the pattern “A; if A then B; therefore B”—while rejecting patterns such as Contraposition.

The entry also surveys possible-worlds theories, premise-based theories, probabilistic accounts, belief-revision approaches, and theories based on relevance or difference-making. These approaches ask whether the conditional concerns nearby possibilities, which background assumptions should be kept, how likely B is given A, how beliefs change when A is added, or whether A changes the status of B. The survey also considers how conditionals interact with necessity, possibility, questions, and commands. Its overall lesson is that conditionals are varied and difficult: different theories explain different features,
key_ideas: People use conditionals constantly, but philosophers disagree about the best rules for them.
The simplest rule treats “if A, then B” as false only when A is true and B is false.
That simple rule can make strange everyday statements count as true, even when A and B are unrelated.
Three-valued systems add a third value for a conditional whose “if” part is false or whose status is left open.
Other theories study nearby possible situations, changes in beliefs, probabilities, or whether the first part makes a real difference to the second.
There is no single agreed theory that handles every kind of conditional in every setting.
summaries.why_it_matters: Conditionals guide predictions, explanations, rules, bets, and everyday decisions. Learning their logic shows why a sentence can seem acceptable in a formal system but strange in conversation. It also teaches that changing one rule—such as adding an “undecided” value—can change which arguments count as good. These ideas are useful for understanding careful reasoning without pretending that every “if” sentence works in exactly the same way.

important_terms.definition: A sentence with an “if” part and a “then” part. The first part is connected to the second part in some way.
The “if” part of a conditional. It states the situation we are supposing.
The “then” part of a conditional. It states what is supposed to follow.
A kind of logic that uses three values: true, false, and a third value such as unknown or not settled.
A way of checking whether an argument’s conclusion follows from its starting statements.

questions_to_think_about: If the “if” part of a sentence is false, should the whole sentence be true, false, or neither?
Does “If the ground is wet, then it rained” say more than “The ground is dry or it rained”?
Why might a conditional need to connect its two parts, rather than merely have the right truth values?
Can a rule that works for ordinary “if” sentences also work for “if things had been different” sentences?

summaries.example: Suppose a fair die is rolled. Consider: “If the result is even, then it is a six.” The material conditional treats this as true on outcomes 1, 3, 5, and 6, so its probability is 4/6. But the conditional probability of a six given an even result is only 1/3, because among 2, 4, and 6, only one result is six. The difference illustrates why a formal theory may distinguish a material conditional from a probabilistic or suppositional conditional.
summaries.summary:
The logic of conditionals studies inference involving sentences of the form “if A, then B.” The central difficulty is that ordinary conditionals appear to express more than a relation between the truth values of A and B. The classical material conditional, A ⊃ B, is false only when A is true and B is false. Its truth-functionality makes it valuable for formal reasoning, but it also validates results that sound wrong in natural language: a conditional follows from “not A” alone, from B alone, and its negation commits one to A and not-B. These are often called the paradoxes of material implication. Counterfactuals create another problem, since a false antecedent would make every counterfactual materially true.

The entry first examines three-valued conditionals. A de Finettian table treats A > B as true when A and B are true, false when A is true and B is false, and void when A is false. The void value reflects a suppositional or betting idea: if the antecedent does not occur, the conditional evaluation is canceled. Related systems, including Cooper- and Cantwell-style approaches, assign the middle value differently when A is indeterminate. Consequently, they disagree about principles such as Modus Ponens, Modus Tollens, Contraposition, Conjunctive Sufficiency, and forms of negation commutation. The entry stresses that trivalence is not one theory but a family of systems, with open questions about counterfactuals, modalities, nesting, and finite-valued expressiveness.

The wider survey compares several frameworks. Strict possible-worlds semantics makes a conditional a necessary material implication across accessible worlds. Variably strict semantics instead checks the closest or most relevant A-worlds, using selection functions, similarity orderings, or relative modalists
key_ideas: Classical material implication is truth-functional and mathematically convenient, but it generates familiar paradoxes: a conditional follows from a false antecedent and from its consequent, regardless of topical connection.

Trivalent theories preserve a truth-table style while allowing a conditional to be void when its antecedent is false. Different tables yield different valid inferences, including disagreements about Modus Ponens and negation principles.

Possible-worlds theories distinguish strict conditionals from variably strict conditionals. The latter evaluate the consequent at relevant or closest antecedent-worlds and can reject unrestricted Transitivity, Monotonicity, and Contraposition.

Premise semantics evaluates which background premises can consistently be retained with the antecedent. Its connection with ordering semantics shows that different presentations can produce corresponding results.
Probabilistic approaches often connect the assertability of A > B with Pr(B|A), but extending that idea to nested conditionals leads to important triviality results and technical difficulties.

Belief revision, relevance-based theories, and accounts of modality or speech acts show that the logic may depend on whether a conditional asserts, supposes, updates, commands, asks, or expresses a dependence.
summaries.why_it_matters: Conditional reasoning appears in mathematics, science, law, computer systems, prediction, explanation, and ordinary conversation. The entry matters because it reveals that “if” is not governed by one uncontested pattern. A formal system may be elegant yet misrepresent relevance; a probabilistic account may model uncertainty yet face problems with nested conditionals; a possible-worlds account may represent counterfactual dependence yet require a theory of similarity. Comparing these approaches helps students evaluate arguments by asking what kind of conditional is being used, what counts as background information, and whether the antecedent genuinely changes the consequent.

important_terms.definition: A sentence of the form “if A, then B,” whose interpretation may involve truth, supposition, probability, belief change, or a relation between A and B.
The condition introduced by “if”; in A > B, A is the antecedent.
What the conditional says follows from its antecedent; in A > B, B is the consequent.
The classical analysis A ⊃ B, which is false only when A is true and B is false. It is also called material implication.
A semantics assigning three values, commonly true, false, and indeterminate or void, rather than only two.
A framework in which the truth of A > B is evaluated by considering relevant possible worlds, often the closest A-worlds.
The idea that A is hypothetically added to an agent’s beliefs to determine what would then be accepted about B.
A conditional whose antecedent is relevant because it changes the truth, probability, support, or acceptance of its consequent.

questions_to_think_about: Is the material conditional a useful idealization, even if it does not capture every ordinary use of “if”?
Should a conditional with a false antecedent be true, false, or indeterminate? What would each choice explain?
Why might the inference from A > B and B > C to A > C fail for closest-world or probabilistic interpretations?
Does high Pr(B|A) suffice for asserting A > B, or must A also raise the probability of B?
What does the failure of a principle such as Import-Export reveal about nested conditionals?

summaries.example: A teacher says, “If the school team wins, we will have a celebration.” The team does not win. Is the statement now true because its condition failed, false because no celebration happened, or simply not settled? A three-valued theory can call it “void” rather than forcing it into true or false. But another theory might evaluate it using likely situations or the speaker’s background assumptions, producing a different result.
summaries.summary:
The logic of conditionals examines how we should reason with “if–then” sentences. These sentences are common, but philosophers disagree about what they mean and which inference rules they support. The simplest approach is material implication. It treats “If A, then B” as equivalent to “Not A or B.” That rule is easy to calculate and works well in parts of mathematics. However, it has surprising consequences in ordinary language. It says that a conditional is true whenever A is false, even if A and B have no meaningful connection. It also says that B by itself is enough to make “If A, then B” true.

Three-valued logics respond by adding a third status, often called void, null, or indeterminate. On one influential table, the conditional is true when both A and B are true, false when A is true and B is false, and void when A is false. This can represent the thought that a conditional is like a bet that is canceled when its condition does not happen. Other three-valued systems handle the middle case differently. As a result, they disagree over important rules. Some support Modus Ponens, the move from A and A > B to B. Others reject it. Modus Tollens and Contraposition do not automatically survive in these systems.

The entry then compares broader approaches. Possible-world semantics evaluates conditionals by looking at accessible situations or at the closest situations where the antecedent is true. Premise semantics instead starts with a set of facts or beliefs and asks which of them can consistently remain when A is assumed. These theories can explain why context affects the result. Probabilistic theories connect conditionals with conditional probability, Pr(B given A), and belief-revision theories use a “Ramsey test”: temporarily add A to one’s beliefs and see whether B

key_ideas: The entry surveys many theories because ordinary conditionals can be used for prediction, explanation, rules, counterfactual imagination, and reasoning under uncertainty.
Material implication is simple and useful, but it can make unrelated conditionals true merely because their antecedent is false or their consequent is true.
Three-valued logics treat some conditionals as void or indeterminate. Different systems preserve different familiar reasoning rules.
Possible-world theories ask which worlds or situations should count as relevant, especially the closest ones where the antecedent holds.
Premise semantics asks which background facts can be kept when we imagine the antecedent. Probabilistic theories compare the chance of the consequent given the antecedent with its ordinary chance.
Some philosophers argue that a good conditional needs relevance: the antecedent should make a difference to the consequent rather than merely being associated with it.
summaries.why_it_matters: Conditional logic helps explain disagreements in everyday reasoning. Someone may treat a sentence as a strict rule, while someone else hears it as a prediction, a guess, or a claim about what would happen under changed circumstances. The topic also connects philosophy with mathematics, probability, language, and computer reasoning. Studying the competing theories encourages careful questions about hidden assumptions, relevance, uncertainty, and the kind of “if” statement under discussion.

important_terms.definition: An “if–then” sentence used to connect a condition with a result.
The “if” clause: the situation being assumed or considered.
The “then” clause: what is said to follow from the antecedent.
A simple two-choice system in which statements receive only true or false.
A logic with three possible values, often true, false, and void or indeterminate.
A rule saying that a conditional is false only when its antecedent is true and its consequent is false.
A method that tests a conditional by considering what happens in relevant alternative situations.
A reasoning rule that allows beliefs to be reconsidered after a new assumption is added.

questions_to_think_about: Why might two people agree that A is false but disagree about the status of “If A, then B”?
When we imagine a different situation, which real-world facts should we keep and which should we change?
Can “If A, then B” be strong even when B is already very likely without A?
Why might a chain of two conditionals fail to support a third conditional?
Should the same logic cover predictions, counterfactuals, questions, and commands?
